signal.title: [Data] Fix ResourceBudget backpressure causing pipeline stall
signal.text: ## Why are these changes needed? Two interacting bugs in `ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy` can cause a Ray Data pipeline to stall indefinitely — CPU/GPU idle, Object Store filling up, no error logged, no progress. Reproducing this requires enough intermediate output to pressure the Object Store; small pipelines won't hit it. ### Background `ResourceBudgetBackpressurePolicy` blocks an operator from submitting new tasks when **either**: (a) the operator's `incremental_resource_usage` (CPU/GPU/memory) exceeds its budget, or (b) the operator's Object Store budget for task outputs is below `obj_store_mem_max_pending_output_per_task`. When either fires, the operator enters `backpressured:tasks(ResourceBudget)` and stops scheduling. ### The two bugs **Bug 1 — `OutputBackpressureGuard.should_unblock` doesn't distinguish Object Store–blocked from CPU/GPU-blocked.** The liveness relaxation in `should_unblock` relaxes an upstream operator's output backpressure when a downstream operator has no active tasks and can't submit — so upstream can finish and release CPU/GPU/memory. This helps when downstream is blocked on condition (a). But when downstream is blocked on condition (b) — its Object Store budget for task outputs is exhausted — relaxing upstream only writes *more* output into the already-full store while downstream still can't schedule. The relaxation feeds the stall it's meant to prevent. **Bug 2 — `update_budgets` unconditionally allocates shared resources to over-reserved operators.** Each scheduling iteration, `update_budgets` recomputes every eligible operator's budget as its unused reservation plus a share of the remaining shared resources. Even when an operator's Object Store usage already exceeds its reserved resources (unused reservation is zero), it still receives a share of the remaining shared resources — restoring a positive budget, letting it submit more tasks, and further draining the shared resources that other operators depend on. **How they compound:** Bug 2 keeps the upstream operator's budget alive so it keeps producing output. Bug 1 relaxes the upstream's output backpressure so that output flows unchecked. Together, the Object Store fills until every operator's budget is exhausted and the pipeline stalls. ## Fix 1. In `can_submit_new_task`, when an operator is blocked on condition (b) but sits idle with input already queued, admit one task so it consumes what it holds instead of relaxing upstream to push more into an already-full store. Bounded to one task per operator (`num_active_tasks() == 0`) and only while the execution is under Object Store memory pressure, so the default path is unchanged and recovery doesn't rest on `IdleDetector` alone. `should_unblock` is left untouched. An earlier revision instead suppressed the relaxation inside `should_unblock` with a `continue`. That left `IdleDetector` as the only recovery path — one block per `DETECTION_INTERVAL_S = 10.0` — and failed `test_e2e_liveness_with_output_backpressure_edge_case` 2/2 in premerge, where 100 blocks would need ~1000s against a 180s timeout. 2. Optionally withhold shared Object Store resources from operators that satisfy **both**: (a) per-operator usage exceeds `object_store_reservation_overshoot_ratio` × its total reserved resources (task-side + output-side), AND (b) this execution's Object Store usage exceeds `object_store_memory_pressure_fraction` of its limit. Both thresholds must be set to enable the throttle; either being `None` (default) preserves legacy behavior. Requiring both conditions avoids throttling when the Object Store is nearly empty (a single overshooting operator is harmless there) and avoids letting one operator drain the shared pool when the store is under pressure — a single threshold would misfire in one direction or the other. Fix 2 pre-filters over-reserved operators before the shared-resource allocation loop (rather than skipping with `continue` inside the loop), keeping the per-operator share fraction aligned with the number of operators actually receiving resources. The fallback branch also iterates the pre-filtered list, preventing leftover budget from being routed back to an over-reserved operator. ## Related issues None. ## Additional information **Enabling the throttle (Fix 2)** — off by default. To enable, set both thresholds on `DataContext`: ```python ctx = ray.data.DataContext.get_current() ctx.object_store_reservation_overshoot_ratio = 1.5 # per-op overshoot headroom ctx.object_store_memory_pressure_fraction = 0.8 # engage at 80% usage ``` Or via environment variables (equivalent): ```bash export RAY_DATA_OBJECT_STORE_RESERVATION_OVERSHOOT_RATIO=1.5 export RAY_DATA_OBJECT_STORE_MEMORY_PRESSURE_FRACTION=0.8 ```

signal.text: ## Description Adds first-class Anthropic Messages API support to Ray Serve LLM for vLLM-based deployments. This allows Anthropic-compatible clients, including Claude Code, to communicate directly with Ray Serve LLM without an additional translation proxy such as LiteLLM or Claude Code Router. The initial implementation supports: - `POST /v1/messages` - `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` - Streaming and non-streaming message responses. - Standard ingress and direct-streaming deployments. - **Vanilla vLLM deployments.** SGlang fallbacks on import failure, P/D disaggregation and data parallel deployments are outside this PR's scope. ## Related issues - Closes #64965 ## Implementation - Added Ray wrappers and alpha public APIs for vLLM's Anthropic request, response, token-counting, and error models. - Extended `LLMEngine`, `LLMServerProtocol`, and `LLMServer` with `messages` and `count_tokens` operations. - Initialized and delegated requests to vLLM's `AnthropicServingMessages`. - Added `AnthropicIngress` (which inherits from `OpenaiIngress`), reusing the existing ingress model resolution, LoRA routing, handle caching, session affinity, and deployment configuration. - Translateed internal vLLM errors into Anthropic-compatible error payloads at the HTTP boundary. - Preserved vLLM-generated Anthropic SSE events for streaming responses. - Added `build_anthropic_app` with support for both standard ingress and direct streaming. - signal.title: [Core][Data][CoreWorker]Discussion: remaining gRPC thread amplification with many task workers per node
signal.text: ### Description ## What happened + What you expected to happen We are investigating unexpectedly high native thread counts in Ray Data task workers on Ray **2.55.1**. Ray has already made several improvements related to worker thread counts: - #54988 / #36936 added `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads`, allowing Raylet to pass a gRPC internal CPU-count hint to worker processes. - #58771 / #58351 introduced `RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread` and reduced the default CoreWorker gRPC reply executor to 2 threads. - #63685 later added cgroup-aware CPU sizing for several RayConfig-based thread pools. These changes are helpful. However, in our workload, a high worker-density node can still accumulate a large number of process-local gRPC-related threads. This issue is not requesting that CoreWorkers share a single RPC endpoint. We understand that each CoreWorker needs an independent endpoint for worker-to-worker direct calls, actor/task RPC, and process-level failure isolation. Our concern is the node-level multiplication effect: ```text number of worker processes × per-worker gRPC/runtime thread count ``` When a high-core node runs many one-CPU worker processes, each process brings its own gRPC runtime and associated native threads. Even after applying the existing worker gRPC CPU hint, the aggregate Pod-level thread count remains high. ## Environment - Ray version: `2.55.1` - Workload: Ray Data task workers - One worker Pod - Pod resources: `50 CPU / 500 GB memory` - Normal Ray task workers: `num_cpus=1` - Concurrent task workers: approximately `49` - Workload concurrency, input size, and Pod resource configuration were held constant across experiments. ## Measurements We sampled representative worker processes and grouped native threads by Linux thread name. | Configuration | `event_engine` threads | `nexting_thread` threads | Total threads per representative worker | Peak Pod thread count | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Default | 32 | 16 | ~341 | ~7200 | | `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4` | 20 | 2 | ~115 | ~5800 | The setting reduced peak Pod thread count by approximately **19%**. We did not observe an obvious throughput or latency regression in this workload. The thread-name counts above were collected from the operating system. We would appreciate confirmation of the exact gRPC / Ray components corresponding to the observed names, especially `event_engine` and `nexting_thread`. For example, the thread names were collected with commands similar to: ```bash ps -L -p <pid> -o tid,comm ``` or: ```bash for task in /proc/<pid>/task/*; do cat "$task/comm" done | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr ``` ## Relevant configuration path Our understanding of the current worker-side configuration path is: ```text RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads ↓ Raylet worker startup ↓ RAY_num_grpc_internal_threads in the spawned worker environment ↓ Ray-patched gRPC CPU-count detection ↓ gRPC internal runtime / EventEngine sizing ``` We also understand that the CoreWorker server-call reply executor is separately controlled by: ```text RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread ``` and defaults to a small value in current Ray versions. This appears to be an important improvement, but it seems to cover the CoreWorker server-call reply executor rather than all possible gRPC EventEngine/runtime thread sources. ## Why this matters For a high-core node with many one-CPU worker processes, the per-process overhead can still become significant at node level. For illustration, consider a hypothetical 192-CPU node running approximately 192 worker processes. Using the observed thread-name counts above: ```text Default: 192 × (32 event_engine + 16 nexting_thread) ≈ 9216 threads ``` With the reduced gRPC CPU hint: ```text RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4: 192 × (20 event_engine + 2 nexting_thread) ≈ 4224 threads ``` These are not exact predictions for every workload or deployment, but they show the multiplication effect. Even mostly idle native threads consume operational budget through: - PID / cgroup `pids.max` usage; - native thread stack reservation and memory overhead; - scheduler overhead; - thread startup and teardown overhead; - increased risk of `pthread_create` / `EAGAIN` failures. This is especially concerning because related reports have already observed worker startup or thread creation failures on high-core systems: - #48700 - #54225 - #59626 ## What we tried We set the following before starting Ray workers: ```bash export RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 ``` This materially reduced worker and Pod thread count without an obvious workload-level performance regression. However, this setting changes a gRPC CPU-count hint rather than expressing a direct worker thread budget. It is therefore difficult for us to know: - whether it is intended as a supported production tuning interface; - which exact gRPC components it changes; - whether it limits initial thread creation only or also runtime growth; - and what values are expected to be safe for different workload types. ## Discussion We would appreciate feedback from Ray maintainers and the community on how this behavior is intended to work and how it should be approached. We understand that each CoreWorker needs an independent RPC endpoint and process-level isolation. We are not assuming that worker processes should necessarily share a single RPC endpoint or that there is one simple solution for all workloads. Our main concern is the node-level multiplication effect: when a high-core node runs many one-CPU worker processes, each process brings its own gRPC runtime and related threads. Even after applying the existing worker gRPC CPU hint, the aggregate thread count can remain large. We would like to better understand the current design, expected operating envelope, and the tradeoffs involved. Questions we would especially appreciate help with: 1. Is `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads` intended to be a supported production tuning knob for worker processes, or should it be considered an internal escape hatch? 2. Can maintainers clarify which thread pools or gRPC subsystems are affected by: - `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads` - `RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread` - `RAY_num_server_call_thread` 3. In particular, does `RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads`: - affect EventEngine initial thread creation; - constrain EventEngine growth; - affect every EventEngine instance in a CoreWorker process; - or affect only some gRPC subsystems? 4. Is there an existing supported way to set a direct per-CoreWorker limit for EventEngine or other gRPC runtime threads, rather than indirectly changing the gRPC CPU-count hint? 5. For high worker-density nodes, are there existing capacity guidelines or tested configurations covering: - one or approximately one worker per CPU; - high-core hosts; - many Ray Data task workers in a single Pod; - expected worker and Pod thread counts; - `pids.max`, `ulimit -u`, and native-thread stack considerations? 6. Does the cgroup-aware CPU sizing work from #63685 also apply to the CPU count seen by the patched gRPC runtime in workers? If not, is that an area where the current behavior could be improved? Potential areas for discussion might include: - clearer documentation and observability for the existing worker-side thread controls; - a direct per-worker gRPC / EventEngine thread limit; - more conservative defaults for CPU-count-driven gRPC internals in task workers; - a per-node budget or admission mechanism for worker-side RPC threads; - automatic sizing that considers cgroup limits and worker density; - or, where compatible with process isolation and fault-tolerance requirements, consolidation or sharing of selected transport/event-loop resources. We are not proposing a specific architecture here. We would like to understand which directions are technically realistic and aligned with Ray's design goals. ## Willingness to contribute We are happy to help investigate and validate this. If there is a preferred benchmark, diagnostic format, or specific hypothesis the community would like tested, we would be happy to run it and report the results. ## Additional measurements we can provide We can provide the same workload and thread-name breakdown for a matrix such as: ```text default RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=1 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=2 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=1 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=2 RAY_worker_num_grpc_internal_threads=4 RAY_core_worker_num_server_call_thread=1 ``` We can also compare the results across Ray versions, including a version that contains #63685. ## Related issues and PRs Issues: - #36936 — Too many threads in Ray worker - #48700 — Ray crashes when too many cores are visible - #54225 — Thread creation error, even with environment variables all set to 1 - #55215 — Make third party library thread count static in worker - #58351 — Same actor/task has different number of threads in different environments - #59626 — Resource exhaustion / `pthread_create` failures in a Ray workload - #63476 — Default GCS thread number considers cgroup Pull requests: - #54988 — Configurable worker gRPC internal thread count - #58771 — Limit CoreWorker gRPC reply threads to 2 by default - #63685 — Consider cgroup limit when fetching CPU ### Use case _No response_

signal.title: [Core] Actor RSS does not drop even if all object refs are released
signal.text: ### What happened + What you expected to happen I created an actor with a function `get`. Each `get` constructs a torch tensor. Driver calls its `get` function for 3000 times and get the results. After clearing all the object refs, the actor rss memory should drop but it didn't. #### memray graph ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0f654e39-b158-4f53-b589-13cfac85b190) #### pmap check After seeing "done!" (i.e. all the object refs should be released), I `pmap -x <pid>` the actor process and found plasma mmap shared memory occupies about 2.6g rss memory. I guess the objects are not released (or fd are not unmapped). #### raylet log Another discovery is the raylet debug log. I checked the logic of `MarkObjectAsUnused`, which tells the client to munmap the object only when ref count = 0. However, all objects in raylet log shows `should_unmap = 0`. Since no more logs about real ref count in `MarkObjectAsUnused`, I can hardly tell if it works as expected. ``` [2025-05-23 14:51:57,409 D 1580641 1580721] (raylet) store.cc:258: Object 00ef45ccd0112571ffffffffffffffffffffffff0100000004e1f505 no longer in use by client, should_unmap = 0 ``` Related code: ```c++ // ray-master\src\ray\object_manager\plasma\connection.h bool MarkObjectAsUnused(const ray::ObjectID &object_id) override { // ... size_t &ref_cnt = ref_cnt_iter->second; RAY_CHECK_GT(ref_cnt, static_cast<size_t>(0)); ref_cnt -= 1; if (ref_cnt == 0) { fallback_allocated_fds_ref_count_.erase(ref_cnt_iter); used_fds_.erase(fd); // Next SendFd call will send this fd again. return true; } ``` ```c++ // ray-master\src\ray\object_manager\plasma\store.cc bool PlasmaStore::RemoveFromClientObjectIds(const ObjectID &object_id, const std::shared_ptr<Client> &client) { auto &object_ids = client->GetObjectIDs(); auto it = object_ids.find(object_id); if (it != object_ids.end()) { bool should_unmap = client->MarkObjectAsUnused(object_id); RAY_LOG(DEBUG) << "Object " << object_id << " no longer in use by client, should_unmap = " << should_unmap; // Decrease reference count. object_lifecycle_mgr_.RemoveReference(object_id); ``` #### core worker log From the perspective of core-worker, no munmap log ("ClientMmapTableEntry dtor munmaped ") is observed. Related code: ```c++ ClientMmapTableEntry::~ClientMmapTableEntry() { #ifdef _WIN32 r = UnmapViewOfFile(pointer_) ? 0 : -1; #else r = munmap(pointer_, length_); #endif if (r != 0) { RAY_LOG(ERROR) << "munmap returned " << r << ", errno = " << errno; } else { RAY_LOG(DEBUG) << "ClientMmapTableEntry dtor munmaped " << fd_.first << ", " << fd_.second << ", addr " << pointer_ << ", size " << length_; } } ``` ### Versions / Dependencies linux x86-64 ray 2.44.1 pytorch 2.6.0 memray 1.17.1 ### Reproduction script ```python import ray import memray import time import os import torch os.environ["RAY_BACKEND_LOG_LEVEL"] = "debug" ray.init() @ray.remote class TD: def __init__(self): memray.Tracker("memray_output.bin").__enter__() def get(self): tensor = torch.randn(262144, dtype=torch.float32) return tensor td_actor = TD.remote() def driver(): results = [] for _ in range(3000): result = td_actor.get.remote() results.append(result) ray.get(results) results.clear() driver() print('done!') time.sleep(60) ray.shutdown() ``` After seeing "done!", try `pmap -x <actor_pid>`. To see memray graphs, type `memray flamegraph memray_output.bin` after the program completes. ### Issue Severity Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

signal.title: [Data] Add a target output file size knob for write ops
signal.text: ## Description Ray Data currently controls Parquet output file sizing through row-based options such as `min_rows_per_file` and `max_rows_per_file`. When row widths vary, files with similar row counts can have significantly different sizes. This PR adds an experimental `target_file_size` argument to `Dataset.write_parquet`. `target_file_size` accepts a positive integer representing bytes. When set, Ray Data coalesces small input blocks until their aggregate in-memory size reaches the target, then sends the resulting bundle to a write task. The implementation: - Adds byte-based rebundling through `EstimateBytes`. - Exposes `Datasink.min_bytes_per_write` for write planning. - Prevents operator fusion from bypassing byte-based rebundling. `target_file_size` is mutually exclusive with: - `min_rows_per_file` - `max_rows_per_file` - `num_rows_per_file` This initial implementation only coalesces small blocks. It does not split an individual block that already exceeds the target. Actual output sizes can also differ because of compression, encoding, and partitioning. Splitting large write inputs can be implemented separately in a follow-up PR. ## Related issues Related to issue [#65327](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65327) ## Additional information

signal.title: [Core] Fix options dropped by actor handles obtained by name
signal.text: ## Description `ray.get_actor(name)` hands back a handle that `CreateInnerActorHandleFromActorData` rebuilds from the `ActorTableData` and `TaskSpec` the GCS returns. Two `ActorHandle` proto fields have no counterpart in either message, so both came back at their proto3 defaults. `enable_tensor_transport` was never set. An actor declared with `enable_tensor_transport=True` reports the option as disabled once another process looks it up by name, so `.options(tensor_transport=...)` on that handle raises `Currently, methods with .options(tensor_transport="...") are not supported when enable_tensor_transport=False. Please set @ray.remote(enable_tensor_transport=True) on the actor class definition.` (`python/ray/actor.py:1124`) even though the class definition already sets it. The same handle works when it reaches another worker as a task argument, because that path deserializes the creator's handle instead of rebuilding it. `max_pending_calls` read a field that nothing writes. It read `ActorCreationTaskSpec.max_pending_calls`, and nothing on the path to the GCS sets that field: `SetActorCreationTaskSpec` does not touch it, and the only writer in the tree is Java's local-mode submitter, whose named actors live in an in-process map and never reach a GCS lookup. The value read back as 0, which makes the `max_pending_calls_ > 0` guard in `ActorTaskSubmitter::PendingTasksFull` (`actor_task_submitter.cc:925`) false, so backpressure was silently off. Both values are already in what the GCS returns. The creator serializes its own complete handle into `ActorCreationTaskSpec.serialized_actor_handle`, and `HandleGetNamedActorInfo` passes that spec back untouched. This PR reads both fields from there. It also checks `ParseFromString`'s result, which the surrounding code discarded. A failed parse leaves the message partially populated, so reading a field out of it can report an option the creator never asked for. The failure path now clears the message and logs at most once a minute. The rate limit matters because the actor name cache is only populated on first task submission, so a worker that only looks the actor up reparses on every call. ### Behavior change The `max_pending_calls` fix changes what users see. `Foo.options(name="x", max_pending_calls=10).remote()` followed by `ray.get_actor("x")` in another process used to accept submissions without bound; it now raises `PendingCallsLimitExceeded` once 10 are in flight. That is what the same handle already did when it arrived as a task argument rather than through a name lookup, so the lookup path was the inconsistent one. ## Related issues Related to #51173, the RFC that introduced tensor transport. Not duplicate work: no open PR touches `src/ray/core_worker/actor_management/`, and searching open PRs for `enable_tensor_transport` and `max_pending_calls` turns up nothing on this path (#59241 adds dtensor serializers, #58556 changes when an actor is marked dead). No open issue describes either symptom. ## Additional information `ActorCreationTaskSpec.max_pending_calls` (`common.proto`) now has no reader in C++ at all; this function was the last one. Java's local-mode submitter still writes it. I left the field alone rather than widen the diff, but it is worth knowing before someone assumes a named lookup can read the value from there. This PR does not fix the pattern that produced the bug. The function fills 18 `ActorHandle` fields one at a time out of two messages that between them do not carry all 18, while the creator's authoritative handle sits in the same spec. Anyone who adds a 19th field to `ActorHandle` without also adding it to `ActorCreationTaskSpec` reproduces this. `enable_tensor_transport` and `max_pending_calls` are two instances of it; a third is `owner_id`, which reads `ActorTableData.parent_id`, a field with no writer under `src/`, though `ActorHandle::GetOwnerId()` has no callers so nothing observes it today. Rebuilding from the serialized handle and overriding only the fields that must come from the GCS would close the whole class, but that needs a separate argument about whether `actor_cursor` and `owner_id` agree between the two views. I put the constraint in a comment above the function instead. ### Tests New `src/ray/core_worker/actor_management/tests/actor_handle_test.cc`, five cases: | Case | What it pins | |---|---| | `NamedLookupPreservesEnableTensorTransport` | Fails without the fix (`Actual: false`) | | `NamedLookupPreservesMaxPendingCalls` | Fails without the fix (`Which is: 0`) | | `NamedLookupKeepsTensorTransportDisabledWhenNotRequested` | Guards against setting the flag unconditionally, or reading it inverted | | `NamedLookupToleratesMissingSerializedHandle` | Empty blob, the one reachable fallback | | `NamedLookupDiscardsUnparseableSerializedHandle` | A payload that parses two fields and then fails; without the `Clear()` the handle reads back `true` and `7` out of the partial parse | Run on macOS (arm64, Apple clang 21, bazel 7.5.0). The two extra flags are local toolchain workarounds unrelated to this change: ``` bazel build --dynamic_mode=off --copt=-Wno-error=deprecated-builtins \ --host_copt=-Wno-error=deprecated-builtins \ //src/ray/core_worker/actor_management/tests:actor_handle_test ./bazel-bin/src/ray/core_worker/actor_management/tests/actor_handle_test ``` ``` [==========] 5 tests from 1 test suite ran. (0 ms total) [ PASSED ] 5 tests. ``` Also run: `actor_manager_test` 10/10, `actor_creator_test` 2/2, `core_worker_test` 36/36. I checked both new assertions in the failing direction by reverting the corresponding line. I did not run an end-to-end Python reproducer; verification here is at the C++ unit level. The Python symptom quoted above is what `actor.py:1124` does given a handle whose flag reads false. Lint: `pre-commit run` for `clang-format`, `cpplint`, `buildifier`, `buildifier-lint`, `trailing-whitespace`, `end-of-file-fixer` and `check-cpp-files-inclusion`, all passing. `cpplint` caught a missing `<utility>` include in the new test, which is fixed. ### AI assistance Written with AI assistance (Claude). I reviewed every changed line, ran the tests above locally, and can defend the change.

signal.title: [Data] Make BigQuery client construction injectable
signal.text: ## Description `ray.data.read_bigquery` and `Dataset.write_bigquery` build their Google Cloud clients through hardcoded private module-level factories in `bigquery_datasource.py`: ```python def _create_client(project_id: str): from google.cloud import bigquery return bigquery.Client(project=project_id, client_info=_create_client_info()) def _create_read_client(): from google.cloud import bigquery_storage return bigquery_storage.BigQueryReadClient(client_info=_create_client_info_gapic()) ``` All five call sites reach these directly — including `BigQueryDatasink`, which reaches across modules into `bigquery_datasource._create_client`. There is no seam for a caller to influence client construction, so today it is impossible to supply explicit credentials (only Application Default Credentials work), set `client_options` for a regional or Private Service Connect endpoint, set a `quota_project_id`, or configure retries and timeouts. The Storage Read API client is worse off than the control-plane client: `_create_read_client()` takes no arguments at all. This PR introduces a `BigQueryClientProvider` abstraction and threads an optional `client_provider` through both public APIs. Omitting it leaves behaviour byte-for-byte unchanged. ## Related issues Closes #65614 ## Additional information ### Why a provider rather than a client instance The obvious API would accept a live `bigquery.Client`. That cannot work here: `BigQueryDatasource` and `BigQueryDatasink` are pickled and shipped to workers, and Google's clients are not serializable — this is the root cause of #45197 (`cannot pickle 'google._upb._message.Descriptor' object`). So the provider is the injected unit. `BigQueryClientProvider` caches the clients it builds and drops them in `__getstate__`, so any subclass is serializable by default and each process lazily rebuilds its own clients. This mirrors the `DatabricksCredentialProvider` pattern already in `ray/data/_internal/datasource/databricks_credentials.py`. ### API ```python class BigQueryClientProvider(ABC): def get_client(self) -> bigquery.Client: ... # cached, control plane def get_read_client(self) -> BigQueryReadClient: ... # cached, data plane @abstractmethod def _build_client(self) -> bigquery.Client: ... @abstractmethod def _build_read_client(self) -> BigQueryReadClient: ... ``` `DefaultBigQueryClientProvider` preserves current behaviour (ADC + the Ray user-agent `client_info`) and additionally accepts `credentials`, `client_options`, `client_kwargs`, and `read_client_kwargs`: ```python ds = ray.data.read_bigquery( project_id="my_project", dataset="my_dataset.my_table", client_provider=DefaultBigQueryClientProvider( project_id="my_project", credentials=credentials ), ) ``` Both classes are exported from `ray.data`, annotated `@PublicAPI(stability="alpha")`, and added to the API docs. ### Backwards compatibility `client_provider` is keyword-only on `read_bigquery` (it falls after the existing `*`). `Dataset.write_bigquery` has no `*` in its signature, so `client_provider` was appended **last**, after `concurrency`, rather than placed next to the related arguments — inserting it mid-list would break positional callers. The private `_create_client` / `_create_read_client` / `_create_client_info*` helpers moved out of `bigquery_datasource` into the new module. They are underscore-private and were only referenced from these two files. ### Testing Eight tests added in `TestBigQueryClientProvider` covering credential and client-option forwarding, kwargs precedence, client caching, cache-dropping across a pickle round-trip, and the read and write paths using an injected provider. The pickle tests are the ones that matter for correctness here, since a provider that serialized its clients would fail on the worker rather than on the driver. ``` python -m pytest python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_bigquery.py 32 passed (24 pre-existing + 8 new) ``` Environment caveat, stated plainly: I do not have a full source build of Ray's C extension on this machine, and the master test conftest chain imports symbols that a nightly `_raylet.so` does not export. The run above was therefore executed against the working-tree `ray/data` on a nightly Ray core, with the three `conftest` star-imports at the top of the test file stripped. The tests themselves and the code under test are unmodified. **`//python/ray/data:test_bigquery` under a real build — i.e. this PR's CI — is the authority, and I will confirm against it once CI reports.** Lint is clean: `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` passes all hooks (ruff, ruff-isort, black, pydoclint, vale, semgrep, docstyle, import order). `ci/lint/check_api_annotations.py` is satisfied — both new public classes carry `@PublicAPI`. ### Duplicate-work check Per `AGENTS.md`, I checked before starting. No open PR touches the BigQuery datasource or datasink (`gh pr list --search "bigquery"` returns only #63070, an unrelated Kinetica connector). The three open BigQuery issues are unrelated to client construction: #44941 (import error), #54288 (docs wording on the 10 GB warning), #45197 (pickling — related as evidence for the design constraint above, but not addressed by this PR). ### AI assistance AI assistance was used to research and implement this change.

signal.title: [Data] Add task-based shuffle v2 support for sort
signal.text: ## Description Previously, sort continued to use the legacy `AllToAllOperator` path when `DataContext.shuffle_strategy` was set to `ShuffleStrategy.HASH_SHUFFLE_V2`. This PR routes sort through the task-based shuffle v2 operators: ```text Input -> SortShuffleMapOp -> ShuffleReduceOp ``` `SortShuffleMapOp` extends `ShuffleMapOp` with range-boundary sampling: 1. Validate the sort key schema and buffer all incoming input bundles. 2. Wait for the upstream operator to finish so every input block contributes to boundary selection. 3. Sample every block with bounded task concurrency based on the available CPU parallelism. 4. Reuse sort v1's sample budget and boundary calculation. 5. Replay the buffered inputs through `ShuffleMapOp` for local sorting and range partitioning. ## Local benchmark Benchmark: ```text release/nightly_tests/dataset/sort_benchmark.py ``` Environment: ```text OS: Ubuntu CPU: Intel Core Ultra 7 265K Physical cores: 20 Threads per core: 1 Runs per configuration: 3 ``` Results are averages over three runs: | Input | Partitions | Legacy time | v2 time | Runtime delta | Legacy object-store peak | v2 object-store peak | Memory delta | Legacy spill | v2 spill | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 5.96 GiB | 64 | 6.401 s | 9.243 s | +44.4% | 12.106 GB | 6.002 GB | -50.4% | 0 GB | 0 GB | | 11.92 GiB | 128 | 20.076 s | 14.377 s | -28.4% | 24.155 GB | 11.989 GB | -50.4% | 27.034 GB | 0 GB | ## Additional information This PR does not change the public `Dataset.sort()` API. The new execution path remains opt-in through `DataContext.shuffle_strategy`.

signal.title: [Core] Store an error when the owner reports an object as FREED
signal.text: ## Description `FutureResolver::ProcessResolvedObject` handles three outcomes of a borrower's `GetObjectStatus` RPC: an unreachable owner stores `OWNER_DIED`, `OUT_OF_SCOPE` stores `OBJECT_DELETED`, and `CREATED` stores the value. `GetObjectStatusReply::ObjectStatus` also has `FREED`, which the owner sends when the object's value was freed while the borrower's reference was still in scope. That status matches no branch, so nothing is put into the memory store and nothing is logged. A `ray.get` on that reference blocks forever with no error. No other path fills the store either. `ResolveFutureAsync` sends one RPC and does not retry. `GetObjects` only falls through to plasma for entries that already exist carrying `IsInPlasmaError`, so a missing entry never gets there. The `OWNER_DIED` put in this function is the only one in the tree, so a later owner death does not help. The pre-ownership raylet code did handle this, treating `FREED` alongside `OUT_OF_SCOPE`: `if (!status.ok() || reply.status() == OUT_OF_SCOPE || reply.status() == FREED) { MarkObjectsAsFailed(OBJECT_UNRECONSTRUCTABLE, ...) }`. That block was deleted wholesale in #14184 and the `FREED` case was never ported to `FutureResolver`. The fix stores `OBJECT_FREED`, which is what the sibling branches do for their statuses. That is also the error the owner already stores locally in `DeleteImpl`, and the one Python maps to `ObjectFreedError`, so the owner and the borrower raise the same exception for the same event. `OBJECT_DELETED` (what the `OUT_OF_SCOPE` sibling uses) would be wrong here, because it maps to `ReferenceCountingAssertionError`, whose message says "This should not happen"; that would report a legitimate user action as an internal Ray invariant violation. ## Related issues Fixes #65269 ## Additional information Adds `future_resolver_test.cc`; this class had no test file. The `FREED` case fails against the unfixed code (nothing is stored, `GetIfExists` returns null) and passes with the fix. I re-verified that by reverting only the production change and re-running. The other two statuses are covered as regression anchors. `bazel test //src/ray/core_worker/tests:future_resolver_test` passes, including under `--config=asan`. Two notes for reviewers. The most familiar trigger, `ray.internal.free`, is deprecated, but the `DeleteObjects` RPC handler and `SealExisting(pin_object=false)` reach the same owner-side freed state and are not. I also left the `if/else` chain as a chain instead of converting it to a `switch` on the enum, to keep this to one concern; a `switch` would stop a future fourth value from being dropped the same way. I used AI assistance to investigate and draft this change. I reviewed every changed line and ran the build and tests myself.

signal.title: [core][joblib] Add opt-in autoscaling to ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool
signal.text: ## Description Closes #31128. `ray.util.multiprocessing.Pool` currently derives a fixed actor count from the CPUs visible when the Pool is constructed. That prevents the Ray Joblib backend from expressing pending demand from a zero-CPU head and from releasing actors after a burst. This PR adds opt-in elastic capacity to the existing Pool. Supplying `min_size`, `max_size`, or `idle_timeout_s` enables elastic mode; `Pool()` and `Pool(processes=N)` keep the existing fixed-pool path. ```python pool = Pool( min_size=0, max_size=64, idle_timeout_s=60, ray_remote_args={"num_cpus": 1}, ) ``` Pool elasticity and Ray cluster autoscaling remain separate. Pool actors retain their existing `num_cpus=0` default. Callers that want pending actors to create cluster-autoscaler demand must request resources explicitly through `ray_remote_args`. The Ray Joblib backend forwards the same options. Joblib's `n_jobs` remains the concurrency ceiling, so `max_size` may lower but never raise it. `RayBackend.configure()` constructs the Ray Pool directly and filters arguments using the installed Joblib and Pool signatures; it does not mutate Joblib's process-global `PicklingPool` inheritance. ## Design The implementation deliberately keeps task scheduling and capacity management separate: - Ray actor mailboxes own queued batches. - The ObjectRef returned by `run_batch.remote()` is the task result protocol. - `_ElasticActorSet` owns only a fixed-size slot table, actor handles, readiness/exit refs, outstanding counts, and idle deadlines. - Existing `AsyncResult`, `IMapIterator`, and `ResultThread` consume ObjectRefs directly. There is no Controller thread, local operation registry, pending-operation deque, result port, or second work queue. ```mermaid flowchart LR Caller["Pool / Joblib caller"] --> Pool["Pool admission lock"] Pool --> Capacity["_ElasticActorSet"] Capacity --> Slots["bounded actor slots"] Slots --> Actors["PoolActor mailboxes"] Actors --> Refs["batch ObjectRefs"] Refs --> Collector["ResultThread"] Collector --> Results["AsyncResult / IMapIterator / callbacks"] Refs -. future completion .-> Capacity ``` ### Actor lifecycle An actor handle is not treated as runnable. `STARTING` owns the handle and readiness ref until `ping()` completes. A slot is never reused while its actor is still exiting. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> EMPTY EMPTY --> STARTING: create actor + submit readiness STARTING --> ACTIVE: readiness succeeds STARTING --> EMPTY: readiness confirms startup failure STARTING --> DRAINING: close or cancel unused pending capacity ACTIVE --> DRAINING: idle deadline, close, or resource handoff ACTIVE --> EMPTY: batch observes actor death DRAINING --> EMPTY: actor exit is confirmed ``` `outstanding` is a count rather than another lifecycle state. Batches can be submitted to `STARTING` actors so the first small task does not pay an additional driver-side readiness round trip. Once any actor is `ACTIVE`, new work prefers active actors. If `max_size` exceeds the resources currently available, a runnable actor with no outstanding work immediately drains when another `STARTING` actor owns work. This event-driven handoff prevents a ready actor from holding the only CPU while work is stranded on a pending actor. With cluster autoscaling, multiple pending actors still expose parallel resource demand and become active as workers arrive. No ObjectRef polling loop is used; readiness, batch completion, and actor exit are driven by Future callbacks, while idle retirement uses a condition-variable deadline. ### Admission, results, and shutdown ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Caller participant P as Pool participant S as ElasticActorSet participant A as PoolActor participant R as ResultThread C->>P: apply_async / map chunk P->>P: check RUNNING under admission lock P->>S: choose or create bounded slot S->>A: run_batch.remote(...) A-->>R: ObjectRef settles with TaskSuccess/TaskFailure[] R-->>C: result or original exception C->>P: close / terminate P->>S: reject new work and drain / kill actors C->>P: join P->>P: return only after every slot is EMPTY ``` Submit and close/terminate share the Pool admission lock. A submit linearizes before close only if its Ray call has been accepted; close queues graceful actor termination after previously accepted actor calls. `terminate()` escalates draining actors with `ray.kill()`. `join()` waits for exit confirmation and therefore cannot make a physical actor slot available early. Worker results use explicit `TaskSuccess` and `TaskFailure` envelopes. Returning an `Exception` object is successful data, while raised exceptions retain their original callback and `get()` behavior. Callback failures are logged without replacing the authoritative task result. Lazy iterators use iteration exhaustion, not a reported `__len__`, as their completion boundary. Closing a Pool preserves already accepted iterator results, publishes one ordered rejection for the next unaccepted chunk, and terminates the collector. A finalizer also stops the collector when the caller abandons an iterator. Readiness/initializer failure is actor-local: the affected ObjectRef reports the failure, the confirmed-dead slot is released, and a later submission can create a replacement. This avoids poisoning healthy actors and avoids an unbounded background retry loop for a permanently bad initializer. ## Class and ownership relationships ```mermaid classDiagram class RayBackend { configure() effective_n_jobs() } class Pool { _pool_lock _elastic_actor_set apply_async() map() imap() } class ElasticActorSet { _condition _slots submit() close() terminate() join() } class ElasticSlot { generation state actor outstanding readiness_ref exit_ref } class PoolActor { ping() run_batch() } class ResultThread { ObjectRef[] refs callbacks } RayBackend --> Pool: constructs Pool *-- ElasticActorSet: elastic mode only ElasticActorSet *-- ElasticSlot ElasticSlot --> PoolActor: uniquely owns handle PoolActor --> ResultThread: batch ObjectRef ``` The slot table is canonical and bounded by `max_size`; callback generation checks reject stale completions. Actor handles and readiness/exit refs have one slot owner. Batch ObjectRefs move directly to their caller-owned result collector. Fixed pools continue to use the existing actor list and replacement behavior. ## Compatibility and explicit tradeoffs - Elastic behavior is opt-in. Fixed Pool construction and scheduling remain on the existing path. - `maxtasksperchild` is rejected in elastic mode because combining task-count recycling with idle retirement would create two competing actor-lifetime owners. Fixed pools retain existing `maxtasksperchild` behavior. - Direct actor-mailbox submission keeps the architecture small and avoids a dispatcher round trip. A finite warm burst submitted before newly pending actors become ready may queue more work on existing active actors; later Joblib dispatch and later Pool submissions use newly active capacity. This is an intentional scheduling/complexity tradeoff, not a correctness dependency. - One daemon `ResultThread` remains per outstanding AsyncResult or iterator, matching the existing Pool callback/blocking model. This PR fixes abandoned lazy-iterator collectors but does not introduce a shared result executor. ## Validation The new autoscaling file contains 28 test functions / 31 collected cases. The final complete run passed: ```text 31 passed in 228.64s ``` Coverage includes deterministic slot transitions, creation/readiness failure, slot reuse only after exit confirmation, initializer retry, actor death, Exception-as-data, callback failure isolation, argument/result serialization failure, graceful close with backlog, forced termination, idle reaping and regrowth, `min_size`, concurrent driver submissions, `max_size` above available resources, lazy `imap` error/close/abandonment, fixed-pool callbacks, Joblib concurrency limits and reuse after failure, and zero-CPU-head demand followed by worker arrival. Additional existing-suite runs: ```text 8 selected multiprocessing/imap compatibility cases passed in 26.75s 5 selected Joblib compatibility cases passed in 40.08s ``` Applicable pre-commit hooks passed, including ruff, black, pydoclint, semgrep, buildifier, import order, and repository checks. `git diff --check` and Python compile checks passed. Commands run in virtual environments against the workspace sources and a locally installed Ray wheel: ```bash pytest python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py -q pytest python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py::test_imap python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py::test_imap_fail_on_non_iterable python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py::test_imap_unordered python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py::test_imap_timeout python/ray/tests/test_multiprocessing.py::test_imap_unordered_timeout -q pytest python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py::test_register_ray python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py::test_ray_backend python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py::test_cross_validation python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py::test_ray_remote_args python/ray/tests/test_joblib.py::test_task_to_actor_assignment -q pre-commit run --files python/ray/util/multiprocessing/pool.py python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py python -m py_compile python/ray/util/multiprocessing/pool.py python/ray/tests/test_joblib_autoscale.py git diff --check ``` The complete existing `test_multiprocessing.py` file was also attempted in the local wheel/source-overlay harness. Its first eight collected cases passed, then `test_callbacks` blocked waiting on its callback queue; that run is not counted as passing. Equivalent fixed-pool success/error callback behavior is covered by the new suite and passed, but the built-source CI run remains authoritative for the complete existing file. ## Duplicate-work check Issue #31128 and open PRs in this area were checked again before this rewrite. #64957 is the only open PR returned for the issue and for Joblib Pool autoscaling; no competing implementation was found. ## AI assistance and human accountability AI assistance was used to develop, review, and test this change. - [ ] The human submitter has reviewed every changed line and can defend the final design and implementation. - [ ] The human submitter has independently confirmed the final test results before requesting maintainer review. This PR remains a draft until both items are complete.

signal.title: [train] Share PlacementGroupCleaner across Train runs
signal.text: ## Description Ray Train v2 currently creates one detached `PlacementGroupCleaner` actor per Train controller. Since cleaners are pinned to the head node, their memory use grows linearly with concurrent Train runs. In the workload described in #65443, 24 cleaners use approximately 14.4 GB on the head node. This PR replaces the per-controller actors with one cluster-wide shared cleaner. The cleaner tracks controllers independently, so a failed controller only triggers cleanup for its own placement groups. The shared cleaner: - uses a fixed, versioned name and internal namespace with `get_if_exists=True`; - remains detached, pinned to the head node, and scheduled outside captured placement groups; - persists controller and placement-group registrations in GCS internal KV; - restores active and incomplete cleanup records after actor restart; - rejects late placement-group registration after controller death; - isolates State API and placement-group cleanup failures between controllers; - scopes State API queries to its own cluster when multiple clusters are active. ## Related issues Fixes #65443. ## Testing ```text PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # 16 passed PYTHONPATH="$PWD/python" python -m pytest -q \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_controller_callback_behaviour.py # 10 passed pre-commit run --files \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/callbacks/placement_group_callback.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/execution/controller/placement_group_cleaner.py \ python/ray/train/v2/_internal/state/util.py \ python/ray/train/v2/tests/test_placement_group_cleaner.py # Passed git diff --check origin/master...HEAD # Passed ``` A local end-to-end multi-job scenario used two independent drivers, each running a real Train v2 `DataParallelTrainer` with a controller, worker, and placement group. Both runs shared one cleaner. After one driver was killed, only its placement group was removed; the other run remained active and completed normally. The cleaner stayed alive throughout. ## Contribution notes No other open PR referencing #65443 or matching this PlacementGroupCleaner change was found before requesting review. AI assistance was used for implementation, testing, and self-review of this change.

signal.title: [Data] Support refreshing vended-credentials for native catalog Iceberg path
signal.text: ### Description Databricks UC vends short-lived storage credentials with 1h TTL. This means any long-running Ray Data job will fail to write to Iceberg tables after that. 2 approaches I can think of - **Workaround (bypass vending)**: sending `header.X-Iceberg-Access-Delegation: ""` [defaults to `vended-credentials`](https://py.iceberg.apache.org/configuration/) and injecting the cloud's storage config so the backend falls through to the job identity's own refreshable credential chain. The native catalog cannot express this as it hardcodes the header https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/227da64f41c387e82a01293f062d68382cc89c16/python/ray/data/catalog.py#L286 - **Correct fix**: vended credentials are short-lived *by design* (least-privilege), so any path that resolves once on the driver and pickles `catalog_kwargs` into write tasks will hit a TTL on a long run. Moving `catalog.resolve()` into each read/write task should fix this. ### Use case A long-running batch-inference job that writes the output to an Iceberg table. This would require a single `write_iceberg` that has a data-file phase lasts more than 1h.
signal.author: nkvuong

signal.title: [Data] Make BigQuery (GCP) client construction injectable in read_bigquery / write_bigquery
signal.text: ### Description `ray.data.read_bigquery` and `Dataset.write_bigquery` construct their Google Cloud clients through hardcoded private module-level factories in `python/ray/data/_internal/datasource/bigquery_datasource.py`: ```python def _create_client(project_id: str): from google.cloud import bigquery return bigquery.Client(project=project_id, client_info=_create_client_info()) def _create_read_client(): from google.cloud import bigquery_storage return bigquery_storage.BigQueryReadClient(client_info=_create_client_info_gapic()) ``` Every call site — `BigQueryDatasource.get_read_tasks`, `BigQueryDatasource._validate_dataset_table_exist`, `BigQueryDatasink.on_write_start`, and the per-block write task (which reaches across modules into `bigquery_datasource._create_client`) — calls these directly. There is no seam for the caller to influence client construction. Concretely, this means a user of `read_bigquery` / `write_bigquery` cannot: - **Pass explicit credentials.** Only Application Default Credentials work. Impersonated service accounts, a `google.oauth2.service_account.Credentials` loaded from a secret manager, or per-dataset credentials in a multi-tenant job are all impossible without mutating process-global ADC state (`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`), which is process-wide and racy when several datasets in one job target different projects. - **Set `client_options`.** No way to point at a regional endpoint (`api_endpoint`), use a Private Service Connect endpoint, or set `quota_project_id`. - **Tune the client.** Custom `google.api_core.retry.Retry` policies, timeouts, or a custom transport / `requests.Session` are unreachable. - **Configure the Storage Read API client at all.** `_create_read_client()` accepts no arguments whatsoever — only `client_info` is set. Credentials, `client_options`, and transport are all unreachable for the data-plane client, even though it is the client that does the actual bulk read inside every read task. - **Test without monkeypatching.** `python/ray/data/tests/datasource/test_bigquery.py` has to `monkeypatch.setattr(bigquery, "Client", client_mock)` — it patches the vendor library's global namespace because there is no injection point. That is fragile and leaks across the module boundary between the datasink and the datasource. Ray Data already has a precedent for exactly this shape of extensibility: `DatabricksCredentialProvider` in `python/ray/data/_internal/datasource/databricks_credentials.py`, an ABC with concrete implementations, injected via a `credential_provider` argument on `read_databricks_tables`. The BigQuery path has no equivalent. ### Use case I run Ray Data jobs that read from and write to BigQuery projects the job process is not natively authenticated against — credentials are fetched at runtime and differ per dataset within a single job. Today the only way to do this is to mutate `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` before each read, which does not work when two reads against different projects are in flight concurrently, and does not survive being shipped to a worker at all. More broadly, anyone who needs a regional endpoint, a quota project, an impersonated service account, or custom retry behaviour on the BigQuery client currently has to fork the datasource. ### Proposed direction Introduce a `BigQueryClientProvider` abstraction, mirroring the existing `DatabricksCredentialProvider` pattern: - An ABC exposing `get_client()` (`bigquery.Client`, control plane) and `get_read_client()` (`bigquery_storage.BigQueryReadClient`, data plane). - A default implementation preserving today's behaviour, extended to accept `credentials`, `client_options`, and extra client kwargs, and to correctly pass `project_id` through to the read client. - An optional `client_provider` argument on `read_bigquery` and `write_bigquery`; omitting it keeps the current behaviour exactly. One design constraint worth stating explicitly, because it rules out the obvious alternative of accepting a live client object: **the provider must be the injected unit, not the client.** `BigQueryDatasource` and `BigQueryDatasink` are pickled and shipped to workers, and Google's clients are not serializable — this is the root cause of #45197 (`cannot pickle 'google._upb._message.Descriptor' object`). A provider that constructs clients lazily on the worker and drops any cached client from its pickled state is serializable; a bare `bigquery.Client` is not. The provider ABC also gives users a documented place to build a fully customized client themselves. This would additionally let `test_bigquery.py` inject a fake provider instead of monkeypatching `google.cloud.bigquery.Client` globally. I have a working implementation of this and am happy to open a PR if maintainers agree with the direction. <!-- AI assistance was used in researching and drafting this issue. -->
